Whether kitchen wall art needs to match hardware is one of those questions I get asked more than almost anything else — and the honest answer is: it doesn't have to match exactly, but it absolutely needs to feel connected. The finish of your taps, cabinet handles, and light fittings sets the tone for your whole kitchen, and the art you choose either reinforces that mood or fights against it. Get it right and the room feels intentional; get it wrong and even expensive art looks like an afterthought.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever hung a piece of wall art in your kitchen, stepped back, and thought it looked completely wrong — even though you loved it in the shop? You're not alone, and I can almost guarantee the culprit was a clash with your hardware finish.

Quick answer: Kitchen wall art doesn't need to precisely match your hardware, but the tones, frames, and art style should complement the finish. Warm hardware like brass calls for warm-toned art and frames; cool finishes like chrome or stainless suit cooler palettes and sleeker styles. Mixed-metal kitchens need art that bridges the finishes — think neutral palettes or pieces that echo two of the metals present.

Understanding how kitchen wall art interacts with hardware is really about understanding the visual language of your room. Hardware sets a metallic undertone — warm, cool, or somewhere in between — and art either speaks the same language or disrupts it. If you want to explore unique wall art that works specifically in kitchens, or browse unique home decor pieces that tie a scheme together, it helps to have a clear framework first. That's exactly what this guide gives you.

How to Match Kitchen Wall Art to Hardware Finishes (Brass, Matte Black, Chrome & More)

The key to getting kitchen wall art to match hardware isn't about identical colours — it's about matching the underlying temperature and mood of the finish. Every hardware finish sits somewhere on a warm-to-cool spectrum, and your art choices need to sit on the same side of that line.

Brass and brushed gold are warm and rich. Matte black is dramatic and bold. Chrome and stainless steel are cool and crisp. Brushed nickel sits in the middle — a gentle, versatile grey-silver that plays well with almost anything.

Hardware Finish Quick-Match Guide

  • Brass / Brushed Gold: Warm amber, terracotta, ochre, and cream art tones; wooden or gold-leaf frames
  • Matte Black: High-contrast line art, botanical prints, black-and-white photography; black or dark walnut frames
  • Chrome / Polished Stainless: Cool blues, greys, white, and clean geometric prints; thin silver or white frames
  • Brushed Nickel: Almost anything works — dusty sage, soft blush, warm whites; simple natural wood or pewter frames
  • Copper: Rust, deep teal, forest green, and terracotta art; antique or unlacquered brass frames
  • Oil-Rubbed Bronze: Earthy, moody tones — olive, burgundy, dark cream; dark wood or bronze-toned frames

I once helped a client who had gorgeous unlacquered brass taps and cabinet pulls, but she'd hung a large print in cool icy blues and silver — a piece she genuinely loved. The room felt oddly disjointed and she couldn't work out why. We swapped the print for a warm abstract in ochre and burnt sienna, kept the same frame but spray-painted it gold, and the whole kitchen suddenly felt like it had been designed by one person. Same wall, same hardware — completely different result.

Pro Tip: Hold a swatch or test print next to your actual hardware in different lights before committing. Kitchen lighting is often warm from halogen or cool from LEDs — and both change how a colour reads against a finish.

Mixed-Metal Kitchens: How to Choose Art That Ties Competing Finishes Together

Mixed-metal kitchens are genuinely popular right now — think brushed brass taps paired with matte black handles, or chrome pendants over a copper-accented island. The look is intentional and stylish when done well, but it creates a real challenge for wall art.

The mistake I always see is people trying to match their art frame to just one of the metals present, which makes the other finishes look like an accident rather than a choice. The secret is to use the art as a bridge between them.

How to Choose Art for a Mixed-Metal Kitchen

  • Go neutral in the art palette: Warm off-whites, stone, sand, and soft sage read beautifully against both warm and cool metals
  • Choose frames in a third neutral: Natural wood, white, or even unframed canvas can avoid the "which metal am I matching?" problem entirely
  • Use art that contains multiple tones: An abstract print with both earthy ochre and cooler grey naturally ties warm and cool metals together
  • Lean into the dominant finish: If 70% of your hardware is brass and 30% is black, let the art lean slightly warm — the black becomes an accent
  • Repeat a colour from the art in a small decor item: A terracotta pot or a grey ceramic on the worktop reinforces the connection
  • Avoid art that strongly features one metallic tone: Gold-heavy prints in a mostly-chrome kitchen make the brass look out of place rather than deliberate

One of my favourite mixed-metal kitchens I've worked on had brass taps, brushed nickel handles, and black pendant shades — the owner was convinced she'd made a mistake. We hung a large abstract in muted sage, cream, and a warm greige tone, in a simple natural oak frame. It didn't match any single metal — it related to all three of them. She said it was the first time the kitchen felt like it was "speaking one language."

Pro Tip: If you're stuck on a mixed-metal kitchen, pull a fabric swatch or paint card in warm greige or soft sage and hold it near each of your hardware finishes. If it looks decent with all of them, an art print in that palette will almost certainly work.

Kitchen Wall Art Placement Guide: Where to Hang for Maximum Impact

Even perfect art in the wrong spot won't do what you need it to. Kitchens have very specific wall real estate — and a lot of it is already taken up by cabinets, splashbacks, and appliances. Knowing where to place art is just as important as choosing the right piece.

The most underused spot in almost every kitchen I've visited is the wall above a doorway or the end panel of a run of cabinets. These are natural focal points that most people overlook entirely.

Kitchen Art Placement Rules

  • Eye level is 145–155cm from the floor — hang the centre of your art at this height unless you're placing above a specific piece of furniture
  • Above a breakfast bar or island: Centre the art above the seating, treating the bar like a sofa — keep it at eye level when seated if possible
  • Narrow gaps between cabinets and windows: Use tall portrait-format prints — they make a feature of a tricky narrow wall
  • The wall opposite your cooker or hob: This is where you naturally look while cooking — make it interesting
  • End panels of cabinet runs: Often the most visible surface from the dining or living area — treat it like a gallery wall or hang one strong statement piece
  • Above a doorway: Great for small prints in a cluster or a single landscape-format piece — just keep it above 210cm so it doesn't feel like an obstacle
  • Avoid walls directly behind a hob: Steam and grease will damage art over time — stick to wipeable surfaces or hang art well away from direct cooking zones
Pro Tip: Before you put a single nail in the wall, tape a piece of paper cut to your art's dimensions and live with it for a day. Kitchen light changes dramatically from morning to evening, and what looks right at noon can feel wrong under evening lighting.

Best Art Sizes for Kitchen Walls by Space Type

Size is where so many people go wrong in kitchens. The default is to go too small — a dinky little print that disappears against the cabinetry and does nothing for the room. But going too large without enough wall space creates a cramped, overwhelming feel.

There's a rule of thumb I always use: the art should fill roughly two-thirds of the wall width it's hanging on. That said, kitchens break this rule more than any other room because of how fragmented the wall space tends to be.

Art Size by Kitchen Type

  • Galley kitchen (narrow, linear): Small-to-medium prints, 30×40cm to 40×50cm; use portrait orientation to draw the eye vertically and make the space feel taller
  • Open-plan kitchen-diner: Go bigger — 60×80cm or larger, or a gallery wall cluster spanning 80–100cm wide; the art needs to hold its own against the dining zone
  • Kitchen with a breakfast bar: Medium-format art, 50×70cm, hung at seated eye level; a pair or set of three works well
  • Large kitchen with island: Statement oversized art, 80×100cm or above, on the main focal wall — anything smaller will look lost
  • Small kitchen with limited wall space: Use the end panel of a cabinet run for a single tall print, 30×60cm — it reads like a feature without needing a large blank wall
  • Kitchen-living hybrid: Treat the kitchen wall as an extension of the living room gallery — scale up to match the rest of the space
Real Example: I had a client in a Victorian terraced house with a tiny kitchen — about 2.5 metres wide. She'd bought a 20×20cm square print and it looked like a postage stamp. We replaced it with a tall 30×70cm portrait print on the end wall, and suddenly the kitchen looked much larger and far more considered.

Color Pairing by Hardware Finish: Choosing the Right Art Palette

Colour is probably the single most powerful connection between your hardware and your art — and it works on a level most people don't consciously register. When the tones in your art echo the undertones in your hardware, the eye reads the room as harmonious without knowing exactly why.

I always start by identifying whether a hardware finish is warm or cool at its core, then work outward from there to the art palette. It sounds simple, but it resolves almost every colour clash I've encountered.

Colour Pairings by Hardware Finish

  • Brass / Brushed Gold: Ochre, terracotta, warm cream, sage green, burnt orange, deep teal (as an accent)
  • Matte Black: Off-white, cream, forest green, dusty rose (used boldly), charcoal, raw linen tones
  • Chrome / Polished Stainless: Cool white, pale grey, slate blue, soft sage, navy, and concrete tones
  • Brushed Nickel: Blush, warm white, dusty blue, sage, soft amber — almost any mid-tone palette works
  • Copper: Rust, forest green, deep teal, rich cream, chocolate brown
  • Oil-Rubbed Bronze: Olive, burgundy, dark cream, mushroom, warm tobacco brown
  • Gunmetal / Dark Chrome: Charcoal, pale concrete, navy, cool sage, off-white

The mistake I always see with chrome kitchens is people choosing bright white art that reads as flat and clinical. Chrome has a slightly blue-silver undertone — so prints with a touch of cool grey or slate read as much more alive against it. Even a barely-there hint of blue-grey in the art background changes everything.

Pro Tip: If you're unsure about a colour palette, photograph your hardware close-up and use a free colour-picker tool on your phone to extract the undertone. Match that undertone — not the surface colour — to your art palette.

Budget-Friendly Art Swaps When Remodelling Hardware vs. Replacing Art

Here's a question I get asked a lot: "I'm changing my hardware — do I need to replace all my art?" The answer depends, but it's rarely as expensive or dramatic as people fear. You have options either way.

Changing hardware is usually the bigger financial commitment, especially if you're replacing taps and a sink as well as cabinet handles. Art, on the other hand, can often be tweaked with a frame change or a swap for a print rather than original art — and the effect can be just as good.

Budget Art Refresh Options

  • Reframe existing art: A new frame in a finish that suits your new hardware can transform an existing print — costs far less than new art
  • Swap prints, keep frames: If your frames still work with the new hardware, swap just the prints inside — a digital download and a quality print costs very little
  • Phase the change: Change hardware first, live with the existing art for a few weeks, and see what actually bothers you — you may find less needs changing than you thought
  • Choose art over hardware if budget is tight: New art is almost always cheaper than new hardware and makes an equally visible impact
  • Use the frame as a bridge: A natural wood frame works with brass, brushed nickel, and matte black — it's the most versatile choice if you're planning to change hardware in the future
  • Invest in a neutral art palette: Art in soft neutrals — warm whites, stone, sage — works across multiple hardware finishes so it won't need replacing if you redecorate
Pro Tip: Spray-painting a frame is genuinely underrated. A £5 can of metallic spray paint in a complementary finish can make a charity shop frame look intentional and expensive. I've done it countless times and it works beautifully.

Seasonal or Trend-Proof Art Choices That Outlast Hardware Trends

Hardware trends move faster than most people realise. Brass was the must-have finish a few years ago, matte black took over, and now mixed metals are dominating the conversation. If your wall art is too closely tied to a trend, it can start to look dated the moment that trend turns.

The good news is that certain art styles are genuinely timeless — and they work with almost any hardware finish because they're rooted in something more fundamental than trend cycles.

Trend-Proof Art Choices for Kitchens

  • Botanical and botanical line art: Plants, leaves, and herbs have been used in kitchens for centuries — they'll never feel dated
  • Simple food illustrations: Classic fruit, vegetables, or market-style illustrations in a limited palette are perennial
  • Abstract expressionist prints in neutrals: Beige, cream, warm white, and stone abstracts don't belong to any particular decade
  • Vintage maps or typographic prints: A beautifully designed map of a favourite place or a simple typographic print ages well
  • Black-and-white photography: Landscapes, still life, and architectural photography in monochrome suit almost every hardware finish
  • Handmade ceramic or textile wall art: A hand-thrown wall plaque or a woven wall hanging sits outside trend cycles entirely

I've had clients ask me to help them choose "safe" art that won't need replacing when they eventually upgrade their kitchen. My honest answer is always the same: lean toward organic, nature-inspired subjects in a muted palette, and avoid anything that feels very of-the-moment. A lemon print in a retro style will start to feel like "that 2020 thing" eventually. A clean botanical sketch in a natural oak frame? That's still going to look good in fifteen years.

Pro Tip: When in doubt, go for art you genuinely love rather than art that's "on trend." Personal connection is the most trend-proof quality art can have — and rooms styled around things people actually love always feel more alive than rooms assembled from trend boards.

More About Making Kitchen Wall Art Work With Your Whole Scheme

The real secret to getting kitchen wall art right isn't about following rules to the letter — it's about understanding the visual relationships in your space and making choices that feel coherent.

Hardware is just one piece of the puzzle. Your cabinet colour, worktop material, flooring, and even the ceramics on your open shelves all play into the overall tone of the room. Art that connects to two or three of those elements — not just the hardware — will always feel more considered than art chosen purely on one criterion.

If you're looking for more real-world kitchen art inspiration, the team at Apartment Therapy have put together a genuinely useful visual guide that covers a wide range of styles and room types — worth bookmarking alongside this one: 18 Kitchen Wall Art Ideas to Inspire You.

The thing I always come back to is this: a kitchen should feel like a place someone actually lives in, not a showroom. Art is one of the most powerful ways to inject personality into a functional space — and when it connects to the hardware finish, the palette, and the overall mood you're after, it does that without any effort at all.

Getting Kitchen Wall Art Right: Final Thoughts From Me

If you've made it this far, you're already way ahead of most people who just grab something off the shelf and hope for the best. Getting kitchen wall art to feel connected to your hardware isn't complicated — it just requires a moment of intentional thought before you pick up the hammer.

Start with your hardware finish, identify whether it's warm, cool, or neutral, and let that steer your art palette, frame choice, and art style. If you've got mixed metals, lean on neutral or bridging tones in the art rather than trying to match any single finish. And if budget is tight, remember that a reframed piece or a quality art print in the right palette can do just as much work as expensive original art.

The kitchens that feel really well put-together aren't always the ones with the most expensive art — they're the ones where every choice feels like it was made by the same person, with the same intention. That's entirely achievable whatever your budget or style.

Whether kitchen wall art needs to match hardware is one of those questions I get asked more than almost anything else — and the honest answer is: it doesn't have to match exactly, but it absolutely needs to feel connected. The finish of your taps, cabinet handles, and light fittings sets the tone for your whole kitchen, and the art you choose either reinforces that mood or fights against it. Get it right and the room feels intentional; get it wrong and even expensive art looks like an afterthought.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever hung a piece of wall art in your kitchen, stepped back, and thought it looked completely wrong — even though you loved it in the shop? You're not alone, and I can almost guarantee the culprit was a clash with your hardware finish.

Quick answer: Kitchen wall art doesn't need to precisely match your hardware, but the tones, frames, and art style should complement the finish. Warm hardware like brass calls for warm-toned art and frames; cool finishes like chrome or stainless suit cooler palettes and sleeker styles. Mixed-metal kitchens need art that bridges the finishes — think neutral palettes or pieces that echo two of the metals present.

Understanding how kitchen wall art interacts with hardware is really about understanding the visual language of your room. Hardware sets a metallic undertone — warm, cool, or somewhere in between — and art either speaks the same language or disrupts it. If you want to explore unique wall art that works specifically in kitchens, or browse unique home decor pieces that tie a scheme together, it helps to have a clear framework first. That's exactly what this guide gives you.

How to Match Kitchen Wall Art to Hardware Finishes (Brass, Matte Black, Chrome & More)

The key to getting kitchen wall art to match hardware isn't about identical colours — it's about matching the underlying temperature and mood of the finish. Every hardware finish sits somewhere on a warm-to-cool spectrum, and your art choices need to sit on the same side of that line.

Brass and brushed gold are warm and rich. Matte black is dramatic and bold. Chrome and stainless steel are cool and crisp. Brushed nickel sits in the middle — a gentle, versatile grey-silver that plays well with almost anything.

Hardware Finish Quick-Match Guide

  • Brass / Brushed Gold: Warm amber, terracotta, ochre, and cream art tones; wooden or gold-leaf frames
  • Matte Black: High-contrast line art, botanical prints, black-and-white photography; black or dark walnut frames
  • Chrome / Polished Stainless: Cool blues, greys, white, and clean geometric prints; thin silver or white frames
  • Brushed Nickel: Almost anything works — dusty sage, soft blush, warm whites; simple natural wood or pewter frames
  • Copper: Rust, deep teal, forest green, and terracotta art; antique or unlacquered brass frames
  • Oil-Rubbed Bronze: Earthy, moody tones — olive, burgundy, dark cream; dark wood or bronze-toned frames

I once helped a client who had gorgeous unlacquered brass taps and cabinet pulls, but she'd hung a large print in cool icy blues and silver — a piece she genuinely loved. The room felt oddly disjointed and she couldn't work out why. We swapped the print for a warm abstract in ochre and burnt sienna, kept the same frame but spray-painted it gold, and the whole kitchen suddenly felt like it had been designed by one person. Same wall, same hardware — completely different result.

Pro Tip: Hold a swatch or test print next to your actual hardware in different lights before committing. Kitchen lighting is often warm from halogen or cool from LEDs — and both change how a colour reads against a finish.

Specific Finish-to-Art-Style Pairings: What Actually Works

General rules are helpful, but specific pairings are where the real decisions get made. Each hardware finish has an aesthetic personality, and the art styles that suit it are more particular than just "warm" or "cool."

This is the section I wish more design guides actually covered, because vague advice like "use complementary tones" doesn't help you stand in an art shop wondering whether that linen-textured botanical print works with your brushed gold handles.

We switched to a set of three oversized botanical line drawings in black ink on cream paper, framed in matte black, and the kitchen went from confused to confident instantly.

Mixed-Metal Kitchens: How to Choose Art That Ties Competing Finishes Together

Mixed-metal kitchens are genuinely popular right now — think brushed brass taps paired with matte black handles, or chrome pendants over a copper-accented island. The look is intentional and stylish when done well, but it creates a real challenge for wall art.

The mistake I always see is people trying to match their art frame to just one of the metals present, which makes the other finishes look like an accident rather than a choice. The secret is to use the art as a bridge between them.

How to Choose Art for a Mixed-Metal Kitchen

  • Go neutral in the art palette: Warm off-whites, stone, sand, and soft sage read beautifully against both warm and cool metals
  • Choose frames in a third neutral: Natural wood, white, or even unframed canvas can avoid the "which metal am I matching?" problem entirely
  • Use art that contains multiple tones: An abstract print with both earthy ochre and cooler grey naturally ties warm and cool metals together
  • Lean into the dominant finish: If 70% of your hardware is brass and 30% is black, let the art lean slightly warm — the black becomes an accent
  • Repeat a colour from the art in a small decor item: A terracotta pot or a grey ceramic on the worktop reinforces the connection
  • Avoid art that strongly features one metallic tone: Gold-heavy prints in a mostly-chrome kitchen make the brass look out of place rather than deliberate

One of my favourite mixed-metal kitchens I've worked on had brass taps, brushed nickel handles, and black pendant shades — the owner was convinced she'd made a mistake. We hung a large abstract in muted sage, cream, and a warm greige tone, in a simple natural oak frame. It didn't match any single metal — it related to all three of them. She said it was the first time the kitchen felt like it was "speaking one language."

Pro Tip: If you're stuck on a mixed-metal kitchen, pull a fabric swatch or paint card in warm greige or soft sage and hold it near each of your hardware finishes. If it looks decent with all of them, an art print in that palette will almost certainly work.

Kitchen Wall Art Placement Guide: Where to Hang for Maximum Impact

Even perfect art in the wrong spot won't do what you need it to. Kitchens have very specific wall real estate — and a lot of it is already taken up by cabinets, splashbacks, and appliances. Knowing where to place art is just as important as choosing the right piece.

The most underused spot in almost every kitchen I've visited is the wall above a doorway or the end panel of a run of cabinets. These are natural focal points that most people overlook entirely.

Kitchen Art Placement Rules

  • Eye level is 145–155cm from the floor — hang the centre of your art at this height unless you're placing above a specific piece of furniture
  • Above a breakfast bar or island: Centre the art above the seating, treating the bar like a sofa — keep it at eye level when seated if possible
  • Narrow gaps between cabinets and windows: Use tall portrait-format prints — they make a feature of a tricky narrow wall
  • The wall opposite your cooker or hob: This is where you naturally look while cooking — make it interesting
  • End panels of cabinet runs: Often the most visible surface from the dining or living area — treat it like a gallery wall or hang one strong statement piece
  • Above a doorway: Great for small prints in a cluster or a single landscape-format piece — just keep it above 210cm so it doesn't feel like an obstacle
  • Avoid walls directly behind a hob: Steam and grease will damage art over time — stick to wipeable surfaces or hang art well away from direct cooking zones
Pro Tip: Before you put a single nail in the wall, tape a piece of paper cut to your art's dimensions and live with it for a day. Kitchen light changes dramatically from morning to evening, and what looks right at noon can feel wrong under evening lighting.

Best Art Sizes for Kitchen Walls by Space Type

Size is where so many people go wrong in kitchens. The default is to go too small — a dinky little print that disappears against the cabinetry and does nothing for the room. But going too large without enough wall space creates a cramped, overwhelming feel.

There's a rule of thumb I always use: the art should fill roughly two-thirds of the wall width it's hanging on. That said, kitchens break this rule more than any other room because of how fragmented the wall space tends to be.

Art Size by Kitchen Type

  • Galley kitchen (narrow, linear): Small-to-medium prints, 30×40cm to 40×50cm; use portrait orientation to draw the eye vertically and make the space feel taller
  • Open-plan kitchen-diner: Go bigger — 60×80cm or larger, or a gallery wall cluster spanning 80–100cm wide; the art needs to hold its own against the dining zone
  • Kitchen with a breakfast bar: Medium-format art, 50×70cm, hung at seated eye level; a pair or set of three works well
  • Large kitchen with island: Statement oversized art, 80×100cm or above, on the main focal wall — anything smaller will look lost
  • Small kitchen with limited wall space: Use the end panel of a cabinet run for a single tall print, 30×60cm — it reads like a feature without needing a large blank wall
  • Kitchen-living hybrid: Treat the kitchen wall as an extension of the living room gallery — scale up to match the rest of the space
Real Example: I had a client in a Victorian terraced house with a tiny kitchen — about 2.5 metres wide. She'd bought a 20×20cm square print and it looked like a postage stamp. We replaced it with a tall 30×70cm portrait print on the end wall, and suddenly the kitchen looked much larger and far more considered.

Color Pairing by Hardware Finish: Choosing the Right Art Palette

Colour is probably the single most powerful connection between your hardware and your art — and it works on a level most people don't consciously register. When the tones in your art echo the undertones in your hardware, the eye reads the room as harmonious without knowing exactly why.

I always start by identifying whether a hardware finish is warm or cool at its core, then work outward from there to the art palette. It sounds simple, but it resolves almost every colour clash I've encountered.

Colour Pairings by Hardware Finish

  • Brass / Brushed Gold: Ochre, terracotta, warm cream, sage green, burnt orange, deep teal (as an accent)
  • Matte Black: Off-white, cream, forest green, dusty rose (used boldly), charcoal, raw linen tones
  • Chrome / Polished Stainless: Cool white, pale grey, slate blue, soft sage, navy, and concrete tones
  • Brushed Nickel: Blush, warm white, dusty blue, sage, soft amber — almost any mid-tone palette works
  • Copper: Rust, forest green, deep teal, rich cream, chocolate brown
  • Oil-Rubbed Bronze: Olive, burgundy, dark cream, mushroom, warm tobacco brown
  • Gunmetal / Dark Chrome: Charcoal, pale concrete, navy, cool sage, off-white

The mistake I always see with chrome kitchens is people choosing bright white art that reads as flat and clinical. Chrome has a slightly blue-silver undertone — so prints with a touch of cool grey or slate read as much more alive against it. Even a barely-there hint of blue-grey in the art background changes everything.

Pro Tip: If you're unsure about a colour palette, photograph your hardware close-up and use a free colour-picker tool on your phone to extract the undertone. Match that undertone — not the surface colour — to your art palette.

Budget-Friendly Art Swaps When Remodelling Hardware vs. Replacing Art

Here's a question I get asked a lot: "I'm changing my hardware — do I need to replace all my art?" The answer depends, but it's rarely as expensive or dramatic as people fear. You have options either way.

Changing hardware is usually the bigger financial commitment, especially if you're replacing taps and a sink as well as cabinet handles. Art, on the other hand, can often be tweaked with a frame change or a swap for a print rather than original art — and the effect can be just as good.

Budget Art Refresh Options

  • Reframe existing art: A new frame in a finish that suits your new hardware can transform an existing print — costs far less than new art
  • Swap prints, keep frames: If your frames still work with the new hardware, swap just the prints inside — a digital download and a quality print costs very little
  • Phase the change: Change hardware first, live with the existing art for a few weeks, and see what actually bothers you — you may find less needs changing than you thought
  • Choose art over hardware if budget is tight: New art is almost always cheaper than new hardware and makes an equally visible impact
  • Use the frame as a bridge: A natural wood frame works with brass, brushed nickel, and matte black — it's the most versatile choice if you're planning to change hardware in the future
  • Invest in a neutral art palette: Art in soft neutrals — warm whites, stone, sage — works across multiple hardware finishes so it won't need replacing if you redecorate
Pro Tip: Spray-painting a frame is genuinely underrated. A £5 can of metallic spray paint in a complementary finish can make a charity shop frame look intentional and expensive. I've done it countless times and it works beautifully.

Seasonal or Trend-Proof Art Choices That Outlast Hardware Trends

Hardware trends move faster than most people realise. Brass was the must-have finish a few years ago, matte black took over, and now mixed metals are dominating the conversation. If your wall art is too closely tied to a trend, it can start to look dated the moment that trend turns.

The good news is that certain art styles are genuinely timeless — and they work with almost any hardware finish because they're rooted in something more fundamental than trend cycles.

Trend-Proof Art Choices for Kitchens

  • Botanical and botanical line art: Plants, leaves, and herbs have been used in kitchens for centuries — they'll never feel dated
  • Simple food illustrations: Classic fruit, vegetables, or market-style illustrations in a limited palette are perennial
  • Abstract expressionist prints in neutrals: Beige, cream, warm white, and stone abstracts don't belong to any particular decade
  • Vintage maps or typographic prints: A beautifully designed map of a favourite place or a simple typographic print ages well
  • Black-and-white photography: Landscapes, still life, and architectural photography in monochrome suit almost every hardware finish
  • Handmade ceramic or textile wall art: A hand-thrown wall plaque or a woven wall hanging sits outside trend cycles entirely

I've had clients ask me to help them choose "safe" art that won't need replacing when they eventually upgrade their kitchen. My honest answer is always the same: lean toward organic, nature-inspired subjects in a muted palette, and avoid anything that feels very of-the-moment. A lemon print in a retro style will start to feel like "that 2020 thing" eventually. A clean botanical sketch in a natural oak frame? That's still going to look good in fifteen years.

Pro Tip: When in doubt, go for art you genuinely love rather than art that's "on trend." Personal connection is the most trend-proof quality art can have — and rooms styled around things people actually love always feel more alive than rooms assembled from trend boards.

More About Making Kitchen Wall Art Work With Your Whole Scheme

The real secret to getting kitchen wall art right isn't about following rules to the letter — it's about understanding the visual relationships in your space and making choices that feel coherent.

Hardware is just one piece of the puzzle. Your cabinet colour, worktop material, flooring, and even the ceramics on your open shelves all play into the overall tone of the room. Art that connects to two or three of those elements — not just the hardware — will always feel more considered than art chosen purely on one criterion.

If you're looking for more real-world kitchen art inspiration, the team at Apartment Therapy have put together a genuinely useful visual guide that covers a wide range of styles and room types — worth bookmarking alongside this one: 18 Kitchen Wall Art Ideas to Inspire You.

The thing I always come back to is this: a kitchen should feel like a place someone actually lives in, not a showroom. Art is one of the most powerful ways to inject personality into a functional space — and when it connects to the hardware finish, the palette, and the overall mood you're after, it does that without any effort at all.

WATCH: 200 Modern Kitchen Design Ideas 2024 | Top 8 Kitchen Wall Decor Ideas With Creative Tips And Tricks

Getting Kitchen Wall Art Right: Final Thoughts From Me

If you've made it this far, you're already way ahead of most people who just grab something off the shelf and hope for the best. Getting kitchen wall art to feel connected to your hardware isn't complicated — it just requires a moment of intentional thought before you pick up the hammer.

Start with your hardware finish, identify whether it's warm, cool, or neutral, and let that steer your art palette, frame choice, and art style. If you've got mixed metals, lean on neutral or bridging tones in the art rather than trying to match any single finish. And if budget is tight, remember that a reframed piece or a quality art print in the right palette can do just as much work as expensive original art.

The kitchens that feel really well put-together aren't always the ones with the most expensive art — they're the ones where every choice feels like it was made by the same person, with the same intention. That's entirely achievable whatever your budget or style.

I'd love to know — what's your current hardware finish, and have you found it easy or tricky to find art that works with it? Drop your experience in the comments below.

Choosing a dining room colour palette is one of those decisions that can feel surprisingly overwhelming — but it doesn't have to be. The best dining room colour palette ideas don't start with a paint chart; they start with the things you already love: a piece of wall art, a favourite fabric, or even the colour of your crockery.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in a paint shop holding seventeen sample cards, completely paralysed, wondering why choosing a colour feels harder than assembling flat-pack furniture? I've been there — and so have almost every one of my clients. The good news is that once you start with wall art and decor as your anchor, the whole process gets a lot simpler and a lot more fun.

Quick answer: To choose a dining room colour palette, start with a piece of wall art, a rug, or a fabric you already love and pull two or three colours from it. Then decide whether you want a light and airy feel or something bold and dramatic, and let the room's size and natural light guide how saturated those colours should be.

A dining room colour palette is essentially the full set of colours working together in the space — not just the paint on the walls, but the tones in your furniture, your textiles, your lighting, and your decor accessories. Getting that combination right creates a room that feels intentional rather than thrown together. If you're starting from scratch or refreshing what you have, exploring unique wall art and unique home decor is genuinely one of the best places to find your colour direction before you commit to anything permanent.

Best Colours for a Dining Room by Style and Mood

The right colour for your dining room depends entirely on how you want the room to feel. A colour that reads as sophisticated in one home can feel cold and uninviting in another — it's all about the mood you're after and the style of furniture you're working with.

Think about what happens in your dining room most often. Is it quick weekday suppers, Sunday roasts with the family, or dinner parties with friends? The atmosphere you want to create should drive your colour decisions from the start.

Colour by Style and Mood

  • Warm and welcoming (traditional/country): Terracotta, warm cream, mustard yellow, deep ochre.
  • Cool and calm (contemporary/Scandi): Sage green, dusty blue, warm grey, off-white.
  • Sophisticated and dramatic (maximalist/glam): Deep teal, forest green, midnight navy, aubergine.
  • Fresh and natural (Japandi/biophilic): Stone, warm white, clay, mossy green.
  • Playful and creative (eclectic): Coral, burnt orange, saffron, sunny yellow.
  • Timeless and elegant (classic): Soft white, slate blue, heritage red, charcoal.

I once worked with a client who had a beautiful dark walnut dining table and wanted the room to feel like a proper grown-up space — somewhere that felt different from the rest of the house. We went with a deep, smoky blue-green and paired it with brass light fittings. The transformation was genuinely dramatic, and it didn't require a single piece of new furniture.

Pro Tip: Bring a piece of fabric, a cushion, or even a ceramic bowl from your dining room to the paint shop when you're choosing colours. Seeing the paint chip against something from your actual room is far more useful than comparing chips under shop lighting.

Dining Room Colour Combinations and Pairings

A single colour rarely tells the whole story in a room. The magic happens in the combinations — how two or three colours relate to each other, contrast or complement, and work together across different surfaces and textures.

The simplest way to think about this is to work with a dominant colour (your walls or largest surface), a secondary colour (furniture, curtains, or rug), and an accent colour (smaller decor pieces, candles, artwork details). Keep the ratio roughly 60/30/10 and you'll rarely go wrong.

Accent Walls and Painted Furniture Ideas

An accent wall is one of the most practical tools in a decorator's kit — it lets you bring a bold, saturated colour into a room without the commitment of painting all four walls. In a dining room, the wall behind a sideboard or buffet is usually the most effective spot.

Painted furniture is another avenue that's wildly underused. A dining table or set of chairs painted in a deep, rich colour can do the same job as an accent wall — and you can always repaint them if you change your mind.

Accent Wall and Furniture Painting Ideas

  • Paint the chimney breast or alcove wall in a deep jewel tone while keeping other walls neutral.
  • Use the same colour on both the accent wall and your skirting boards for a more considered, wrapped effect.
  • Paint just the dining chair legs in a contrasting colour (navy legs on a natural wood chair, for instance) — small but impactful.
  • A painted sideboard in sage green or dusty blue instantly anchors the room without touching the walls at all.
  • Try a two-tone wall — paint the lower two-thirds (to dado rail height) in a darker shade and the upper third in a lighter tone.
  • Colour-drenching one corner of a room (walls, trim, and ceiling of that corner in the same shade) creates a cosy, enveloping feel.

A client of mine had a perfectly good sideboard she was about to get rid of because it felt dated. We painted it in a warm terracotta, replaced the handles with brushed brass ones, and it became the focal point of the entire room. She messages me pictures of it regularly — genuinely one of my favourite transformations on a tiny budget.

Real Example: A two-tone wall — darker on the bottom, lighter on top — is a brilliant trick for rooms with low ceilings. The lighter upper tone draws the eye upward and makes the ceiling feel higher, while the darker lower half gives the room a grounded, purposeful feel.

Light and Airy vs Bold and Dramatic Palette Choices

This is the big decision, and it's one where I see people second-guess themselves constantly. Both approaches work brilliantly in a dining room — but they create completely different experiences of the space, and you need to be honest with yourself about which one you actually want to live with.

Light and airy palettes create a sense of space, freshness, and calm. Bold and dramatic palettes create intimacy, warmth, and a sense of occasion. Neither is better — it's entirely about the atmosphere you want to eat and entertain in.

How to Decide Between Light/Airy and Bold/Dramatic

  • Room size: Smaller rooms can handle bold colours beautifully — embracing the cosiness rather than fighting it. Light colours work best in already generous spaces.
  • Natural light: North-facing rooms can feel cold with pale colours; a warm, saturated tone can actually make them feel cosier and more welcoming.
  • How you use the room: If your dining room doubles as a daytime work or study space, lighter palettes are more versatile. For evenings-only entertaining, go bold.
  • Your furniture: Dark, heavy furniture tends to disappear into dark walls (in a good way), while light furniture pops against bold backgrounds.
  • Your personality: Be honest. If you're a cautious decorator who changes their mind often, start lighter. You can always go darker later.
Pro Tip: If you want a bold, dramatic palette but feel nervous, try it on the ceiling first. A deep, rich ceiling colour in an otherwise neutral room creates a cosy, theatrical effect that's far less scary than four dark walls — and the results are usually stunning.

Top Colour Picks by Room Size and Natural Light

Room size and the direction your windows face are two of the most practical constraints in any decorating decision, and they matter enormously in a dining room. The same colour can feel completely different depending on whether the room gets blasting south-facing sun or cool, diffused north-facing light.

Here's how I approach it with every client: we identify which direction the main windows face, how many windows there are, and whether there are any obstructions outside like tall hedges or neighbouring buildings. That tells us a lot before we even look at a paint chip.

How Wall Art and Prints Complement a Dining Room Colour Palette

This is the bit that most decorating guides completely skip over, and honestly it's the part I find most exciting. Wall art isn't just a finishing touch you add once the "real" decorating is done — it can be the very starting point from which your entire colour palette is built.

I always recommend choosing your key piece of wall art before you choose your paint colour. A print or canvas you genuinely love already contains a perfectly balanced colour palette. All you have to do is lift those colours out and apply them to the room around it.

A mixed-race couple — a South Asian woman and a white man, both in their 30s — are standing near the table together looking at paint swatches, comparing them to the ceramic tableware in a natural, candid way.]]

How to Pull a Colour Palette from a Piece of Art

  • Identify the dominant colour in the artwork — this becomes your wall or furniture colour.
  • Find the secondary colour (usually in the mid-tones of the piece) — this works well for textiles like curtains or a rug.
  • Use the accent or highlight colour from the artwork for small decor pieces: candles, ceramics, vases.
  • If the art contains a neutral (cream, warm white, grey), use that for trim, skirting boards, and ceiling.
  • Don't match the art exactly to the wall colour — a small amount of contrast between art and wall makes both look better.
  • Hang art at eye level when seated (around 140–150cm from the floor to the centre of the piece) in a dining room specifically.

The mistake I always see is people buying art to match their existing room rather than letting it lead the room. I had a client who'd repainted her dining room three times in two years trying to find the right colour. Then she bought a large botanical print she adored — and we built the whole room around it in shades of warm cream, deep sage and rust. She hasn't wanted to change anything since.

Pro Tip: If you already have art on your dining room walls, take a photograph of it and use a free colour-picker tool online to identify the exact hex codes of its main colours. You can then take those codes to a paint supplier and find the closest match — it's a far more precise method than eyeballing it.

Certain paint colours have very natural partners when it comes to wall decor, and knowing those combinations in advance saves an enormous amount of trial and error. It's less about rules and more about understanding contrast, warmth, and visual balance.

The key question is always: does the wall decor need to stand out against the wall, or blend harmoniously with it? Both can work — but you need to decide which effect you're going for before you start hanging things.

  • Deep sage green: Pairs beautifully with natural rattan mirrors, terracotta ceramic wall plates, and dried botanicals in earthy frames.
  • Midnight navy: Works brilliantly with gold or brass-finish wall sconces, cream-toned macramé, and warm-toned abstract wall prints in amber or ochre.
  • Warm terracotta: Looks stunning with woven hanging decor, dark wood shelf brackets, and cream or off-white ceramic pieces.
  • Soft warm white: A blank canvas — go for statement pieces with bold colour, natural textures like rattan or linen, or a gallery wall with warm wood frames.
  • Charcoal or near-black: Pair with brushed silver or pewter-finish sconces, light-toned art subjects with warm frames, and trailing plants in white or cream pots.
  • Dusty blush or mauve: Complement with vintage-style botanical prints, gilded-edge mirrors, and soft natural linen wall hangings.
Real Example: A client had painted her dining room in a deep inky green and then bought stark white ceramic wall plates to hang — and the contrast was so harsh it looked clinical. We swapped them for warm cream and terracotta versions instead, and the whole wall came to life. Matching the warmth or coolness of your decor to the underlying tone of your paint colour is the detail that ties a room together.

Colour Palette Ideas by Dining Room Aesthetic

Your dining room's overall aesthetic — the style and design language you're working with — should shape your colour choices as much as the practical factors of light and size. These days there are so many distinct aesthetics to draw from, and each one has a really clear colour language once you know what to look for.

I find it helpful to identify one primary aesthetic and one secondary one, then let those two inform your colour and decor decisions. It stops a room feeling like it's from nowhere — or everywhere at once.

Colour Palettes by Dining Room Aesthetic

  • Minimalist: Warm white, light stone, pale greige. One deliberate accent — a single warm mustard or muted terracotta. Avoid clutter in colour and objects alike.
  • Japandi: Stone, warm cream, warm white, soft sand, with natural wood and muted sage as secondary tones. Nothing high-contrast or bright.
  • Maximalist: Deep, jewel-toned walls (teal, plum, forest green) with layered pattern, gold accents, and rich mixed colours across textiles and art. Clashing is encouraged — deliberately.
  • Cottagecore / country: Warm cream, sage, duck egg blue, warm yellow. Mismatched china, dried flowers, woven textiles, and hand-painted ceramics are your best friends.
  • Industrial: Charcoal, warm grey, raw brick tones, with black metal accents and aged warm-toned wood. Avoid anything soft or pastel.
  • Coastal / nautical: Sandy cream, driftwood grey, soft aqua, navy. Natural textures like seagrass, linen and rattan work alongside muted blues and warm whites.
  • Eclectic / bohemian: Rich saffron, rust, dusty rose, teal, ochre. Layer patterns, mix metals, and embrace art from multiple sources and styles.
Pro Tip: If you're going maximalist, choose one colour as a "hero" that repeats at least three times throughout the room — on a wall, in a textile, and in a decor object. That repetition is what stops a maximalist room from looking chaotic and makes it look curated instead.

Budget-Friendly Ways to Introduce Colour Through Art and Accessories

Paint is brilliant, but it's not the only way to bring colour into a dining room — and for renters, or anyone who's just not ready to commit to a full repaint, art and accessories can do an enormous amount of the heavy lifting.

The principle is simple: colour reads in a room regardless of what surface it's on. A set of terracotta ceramic vases on a sideboard will read as "terracotta dining room" almost as strongly as terracotta walls would. And it costs a fraction of the price, with none of the hassle.

A young Latina woman in her late 20s crouches by the sideboard arranging ceramic pots, candid and natural.]]

Budget Colour Ideas Without Paint

  • Hang a large print or gallery wall as a focal point — even two or three coordinating prints together create a strong colour statement.
  • Layer a colourful rug under the dining table — it defines the zone and introduces colour at floor level without touching the walls.
  • Replace plain dining chair cushions or pads with ones in a bold or contrasting colour.
  • Group ceramic vases, jugs, or candle holders on a sideboard in two or three complementary colours for a curated look.
  • Swap out your pendant light shade for one in a coloured material — terracotta rattan, sage green cotton, or warm amber glass all add instant colour overhead.
  • Invest in coloured linen napkins and a tablecloth — it's the most flexible and cheapest way to shift the colour story of a room seasonally.
  • Add a large woven basket, wall hanging, or macramé piece for warm earthy tones without any commitment.

I always tell renters and first-time decorators: start with a rug and a print. Those two things alone can completely transform the feel of a room. I once turned a completely generic cream-box dining room into something that felt genuinely personal just using a sage green rug, a mustard linen pendant shade, and two large botanical prints on opposite walls. The total spend was less than most people spend on a single tin of specialist paint.

Current and Trending Colour Directions for Dining Rooms

  • Warm earthy tones: Terracotta, warm sand, raw clay, and rust are at the height of their popularity right now — and they photograph beautifully too.
  • Moody deep greens: From sage to forest to emerald, green continues to be the most versatile and trend-resistant colour in interiors.
  • Warm off-whites and putty tones: The move away from cool, stark whites continues — warm plaster tones and limewash finishes are leading the way.
  • Chocolate brown and caramel: Rich warm browns are having a genuine moment in interiors right now — paired with cream and brass, they feel luxurious without being cold.
  • Seasonal shifts through accessories: Keep a neutral or warm base year-round and swap out textiles, candles, and ceramics seasonally — richer tones in autumn and winter, lighter fresher ones in spring and summer.
Pro Tip: For an easy seasonal refresh, keep a box of dining room accessories in seasonal colours. A set of deep burgundy linen napkins and amber glass candle holders can completely shift a room from summer-fresh to autumn-cosy in under ten minutes. Your Dining Room, Your Colour Story

If there's one thing I hope you take away from all of this, it's that choosing a dining room colour palette doesn't have to feel like a high-stakes decision. Start small, start with what you love, and let the room evolve naturally from there.

You don't need to do everything at once. A rug and a print can transform a space. A painted sideboard can change the whole conversation. And when you're ready to paint, you'll be doing it with real confidence because the palette will already feel like yours — not something you borrowed from a paint brand's catalogue.

The most memorable dining rooms I've ever worked in weren't the ones with the biggest budgets or the most perfect colour combinations. They were the ones that felt genuinely lived-in and personal. That's always the goal.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in a paint shop holding seventeen sample cards, completely paralysed, wondering why choosing a colour feels harder than assembling flat-pack furniture? I've been there — and so have almost every one of my clients. The good news is that once you start with wall art and decor as your anchor, the whole process gets a lot simpler and a lot more fun.

Quick answer: To choose a dining room colour palette, start with a piece of wall art, a rug, or a fabric you already love and pull two or three colours from it. Then decide whether you want a light and airy feel or something bold and dramatic, and let the room's size and natural light guide how saturated those colours should be.

A dining room colour palette is essentially the full set of colours working together in the space — not just the paint on the walls, but the tones in your furniture, your textiles, your lighting, and your decor accessories. Getting that combination right creates a room that feels intentional rather than thrown together. If you're starting from scratch or refreshing what you have, exploring unique wall art and unique home decor is genuinely one of the best places to find your colour direction before you commit to anything permanent.

Best Colours for a Dining Room by Style and Mood

The right colour for your dining room depends entirely on how you want the room to feel. A colour that reads as sophisticated in one home can feel cold and uninviting in another — it's all about the mood you're after and the style of furniture you're working with.

Think about what happens in your dining room most often. Is it quick weekday suppers, Sunday roasts with the family, or dinner parties with friends? The atmosphere you want to create should drive your colour decisions from the start.

Colour by Style and Mood

  • Warm and welcoming (traditional/country): Terracotta, warm cream, mustard yellow, deep ochre.
  • Cool and calm (contemporary/Scandi): Sage green, dusty blue, warm grey, off-white.
  • Sophisticated and dramatic (maximalist/glam): Deep teal, forest green, midnight navy, aubergine.
  • Fresh and natural (Japandi/biophilic): Stone, warm white, clay, mossy green.
  • Playful and creative (eclectic): Coral, burnt orange, saffron, sunny yellow.
  • Timeless and elegant (classic): Soft white, slate blue, heritage red, charcoal.

I once worked with a client who had a beautiful dark walnut dining table and wanted the room to feel like a proper grown-up space — somewhere that felt different from the rest of the house. We went with a deep, smoky blue-green and paired it with brass light fittings. The transformation was genuinely dramatic, and it didn't require a single piece of new furniture.

Pro Tip: Bring a piece of fabric, a cushion, or even a ceramic bowl from your dining room to the paint shop when you're choosing colours. Seeing the paint chip against something from your actual room is far more useful than comparing chips under shop lighting.

Dining Room Colour Combinations and Pairings

A single colour rarely tells the whole story in a room. The magic happens in the combinations — how two or three colours relate to each other, contrast or complement, and work together across different surfaces and textures.

The simplest way to think about this is to work with a dominant colour (your walls or largest surface), a secondary colour (furniture, curtains, or rug), and an accent colour (smaller decor pieces, candles, artwork details). Keep the ratio roughly 60/30/10 and you'll rarely go wrong.

Accent Walls and Painted Furniture Ideas

An accent wall is one of the most practical tools in a decorator's kit — it lets you bring a bold, saturated colour into a room without the commitment of painting all four walls. In a dining room, the wall behind a sideboard or buffet is usually the most effective spot.

Painted furniture is another avenue that's wildly underused. A dining table or set of chairs painted in a deep, rich colour can do the same job as an accent wall — and you can always repaint them if you change your mind.

Accent Wall and Furniture Painting Ideas

  • Paint the chimney breast or alcove wall in a deep jewel tone while keeping other walls neutral.
  • Use the same colour on both the accent wall and your skirting boards for a more considered, wrapped effect.
  • Paint just the dining chair legs in a contrasting colour (navy legs on a natural wood chair, for instance) — small but impactful.
  • A painted sideboard in sage green or dusty blue instantly anchors the room without touching the walls at all.
  • Try a two-tone wall — paint the lower two-thirds (to dado rail height) in a darker shade and the upper third in a lighter tone.
  • Colour-drenching one corner of a room (walls, trim, and ceiling of that corner in the same shade) creates a cosy, enveloping feel.

A client of mine had a perfectly good sideboard she was about to get rid of because it felt dated. We painted it in a warm terracotta, replaced the handles with brushed brass ones, and it became the focal point of the entire room. She messages me pictures of it regularly — genuinely one of my favourite transformations on a tiny budget.

Light and Airy vs Bold and Dramatic Palette Choices

This is the big decision, and it's one where I see people second-guess themselves constantly. Both approaches work brilliantly in a dining room — but they create completely different experiences of the space, and you need to be honest with yourself about which one you actually want to live with.

Light and airy palettes create a sense of space, freshness, and calm. Bold and dramatic palettes create intimacy, warmth, and a sense of occasion. Neither is better — it's entirely about the atmosphere you want to eat and entertain in.

How to Decide Between Light/Airy and Bold/Dramatic

  • Room size: Smaller rooms can handle bold colours beautifully — embracing the cosiness rather than fighting it. Light colours work best in already generous spaces.
  • Natural light: North-facing rooms can feel cold with pale colours; a warm, saturated tone can actually make them feel cosier and more welcoming.
  • How you use the room: If your dining room doubles as a daytime work or study space, lighter palettes are more versatile. For evenings-only entertaining, go bold.
  • Your furniture: Dark, heavy furniture tends to disappear into dark walls (in a good way), while light furniture pops against bold backgrounds.
  • Your personality: Be honest. If you're a cautious decorator who changes their mind often, start lighter. You can always go darker later.
Pro Tip: If you want a bold, dramatic palette but feel nervous, try it on the ceiling first. A deep, rich ceiling colour in an otherwise neutral room creates a cosy, theatrical effect that's far less scary than four dark walls — and the results are usually stunning.

Top Colour Picks by Room Size and Natural Light

Room size and the direction your windows face are two of the most practical constraints in any decorating decision, and they matter enormously in a dining room. The same colour can feel completely different depending on whether the room gets blasting south-facing sun or cool, diffused north-facing light.

Here's how I approach it with every client: we identify which direction the main windows face, how many windows there are, and whether there are any obstructions outside like tall hedges or neighbouring buildings. That tells us a lot before we even look at a paint chip.

Room Type Best Colour Choices Colours to Avoid
Small, north-facing Warm terracotta, warm white, soft yellow, deep earthy tones Cool grey, icy blue, stark white
Small, south-facing Soft sage, light blush, warm linen, pale aqua Very dark tones (can feel heavy with strong sun)
Large, north-facing Deep jewel tones, forest green, navy, burnt sienna Very pale, cold shades that make the room feel clinical
Large, south-facing Any colour — lucky you! Bold or light, both work well Nothing to avoid specifically — just ensure tones suit your furniture
Open-plan dining area Consistent neutral base with bold accents in the dining zone Colours that clash with the adjacent living space
Pro Tip: Mirrors are one of the best tricks for making a small, dark dining room feel lighter and larger without changing the colour at all. A round mirror placed opposite a window bounces natural light around the room and adds a decorative element at the same time.

How Wall Art and Prints Complement a Dining Room Colour Palette

This is the bit that most decorating guides completely skip over, and honestly it's the part I find most exciting. Wall art isn't just a finishing touch you add once the "real" decorating is done — it can be the very starting point from which your entire colour palette is built.

I always recommend choosing your key piece of wall art before you choose your paint colour. A print or canvas you genuinely love already contains a perfectly balanced colour palette. All you have to do is lift those colours out and apply them to the room around it.

How to Pull a Colour Palette from a Piece of Art

  • Identify the dominant colour in the artwork — this becomes your wall or furniture colour.
  • Find the secondary colour (usually in the mid-tones of the piece) — this works well for textiles like curtains or a rug.
  • Use the accent or highlight colour from the artwork for small decor pieces: candles, ceramics, vases.
  • If the art contains a neutral (cream, warm white, grey), use that for trim, skirting boards, and ceiling.
  • Don't match the art exactly to the wall colour — a small amount of contrast between art and wall makes both look better.
  • Hang art at eye level when seated (around 140–150cm from the floor to the centre of the piece) in a dining room specifically.

The mistake I always see is people buying art to match their existing room rather than letting it lead the room. I had a client who'd repainted her dining room three times in two years trying to find the right colour. Then she bought a large botanical print she adored — and we built the whole room around it in shades of warm cream, deep sage and rust. She hasn't wanted to change anything since.

Pro Tip: If you already have art on your dining room walls, take a photograph of it and use a free colour-picker tool online to identify the exact hex codes of its main colours. You can then take those codes to a paint supplier and find the closest match — it's a far more precise method than eyeballing it.

Pairing Wall Decor with Specific Paint Colours

Certain paint colours have very natural partners when it comes to wall decor, and knowing those combinations in advance saves an enormous amount of trial and error. It's less about rules and more about understanding contrast, warmth, and visual balance.

The key question is always: does the wall decor need to stand out against the wall, or blend harmoniously with it? Both can work — but you need to decide which effect you're going for before you start hanging things.

Paint Colour to Wall Decor Pairings

  • Deep sage green: Pairs beautifully with natural rattan mirrors, terracotta ceramic wall plates, and dried botanicals in earthy frames.
  • Midnight navy: Works brilliantly with gold or brass-finish wall sconces, cream-toned macramé, and warm-toned abstract wall prints in amber or ochre.
  • Warm terracotta: Looks stunning with woven hanging decor, dark wood shelf brackets, and cream or off-white ceramic pieces.
  • Soft warm white: A blank canvas — go for statement pieces with bold colour, natural textures like rattan or linen, or a gallery wall with warm wood frames.
  • Charcoal or near-black: Pair with brushed silver or pewter-finish sconces, light-toned art subjects with warm frames, and trailing plants in white or cream pots.
  • Dusty blush or mauve: Complement with vintage-style botanical prints, gilded-edge mirrors, and soft natural linen wall hangings.
Real Example: A client had painted her dining room in a deep inky green and then bought stark white ceramic wall plates to hang — and the contrast was so harsh it looked clinical. We swapped them for warm cream and terracotta versions instead, and the whole wall came to life. Matching the warmth or coolness of your decor to the underlying tone of your paint colour is the detail that ties a room together.

Colour Palette Ideas by Dining Room Aesthetic

Your dining room's overall aesthetic — the style and design language you're working with — should shape your colour choices as much as the practical factors of light and size. These days there are so many distinct aesthetics to draw from, and each one has a really clear colour language once you know what to look for.

I find it helpful to identify one primary aesthetic and one secondary one, then let those two inform your colour and decor decisions. It stops a room feeling like it's from nowhere — or everywhere at once.

Colour Palettes by Dining Room Aesthetic

  • Minimalist: Warm white, light stone, pale greige. One deliberate accent — a single warm mustard or muted terracotta. Avoid clutter in colour and objects alike.
  • Japandi: Stone, warm cream, warm white, soft sand, with natural wood and muted sage as secondary tones. Nothing high-contrast or bright.
  • Maximalist: Deep, jewel-toned walls (teal, plum, forest green) with layered pattern, gold accents, and rich mixed colours across textiles and art. Clashing is encouraged — deliberately.
  • Cottagecore / country: Warm cream, sage, duck egg blue, warm yellow. Mismatched china, dried flowers, woven textiles, and hand-painted ceramics are your best friends.
  • Industrial: Charcoal, warm grey, raw brick tones, with black metal accents and aged warm-toned wood. Avoid anything soft or pastel.
  • Coastal / nautical: Sandy cream, driftwood grey, soft aqua, navy. Natural textures like seagrass, linen and rattan work alongside muted blues and warm whites.
  • Eclectic / bohemian: Rich saffron, rust, dusty rose, teal, ochre. Layer patterns, mix metals, and embrace art from multiple sources and styles.
Pro Tip: If you're going maximalist, choose one colour as a "hero" that repeats at least three times throughout the room — on a wall, in a textile, and in a decor object. That repetition is what stops a maximalist room from looking chaotic and makes it look curated instead.

Budget-Friendly Ways to Introduce Colour Through Art and Accessories

Paint is brilliant, but it's not the only way to bring colour into a dining room — and for renters, or anyone who's just not ready to commit to a full repaint, art and accessories can do an enormous amount of the heavy lifting.

The principle is simple: colour reads in a room regardless of what surface it's on. A set of terracotta ceramic vases on a sideboard will read as "terracotta dining room" almost as strongly as terracotta walls would. And it costs a fraction of the price, with none of the hassle.

Budget Colour Ideas Without Paint

  • Hang a large print or gallery wall as a focal point — even two or three coordinating prints together create a strong colour statement.
  • Layer a colourful rug under the dining table — it defines the zone and introduces colour at floor level without touching the walls.
  • Replace plain dining chair cushions or pads with ones in a bold or contrasting colour.
  • Group ceramic vases, jugs, or candle holders on a sideboard in two or three complementary colours for a curated look.
  • Swap out your pendant light shade for one in a coloured material — terracotta rattan, sage green cotton, or warm amber glass all add instant colour overhead.
  • Invest in coloured linen napkins and a tablecloth — it's the most flexible and cheapest way to shift the colour story of a room seasonally.
  • Add a large woven basket, wall hanging, or macramé piece for warm earthy tones without any commitment.

I always tell renters and first-time decorators: start with a rug and a print. Those two things alone can completely transform the feel of a room. I once turned a completely generic cream-box dining room into something that felt genuinely personal just using a sage green rug, a mustard linen pendant shade, and two large botanical prints on opposite walls. The total spend was less than most people spend on a single tin of specialist paint.

Pro Tip: When you're using art and accessories as your main source of colour, pick ONE colour to repeat at least three times across different objects — once in the rug, once in a ceramic, once in a textile. That repetition is what makes a room look styled rather than random.

Seasonal and Trend-Led Dining Room Palettes for Right Now

Colour trends in interiors change more slowly than fashion — a dining room you paint this year isn't going out of style next season. That said, there are some genuinely beautiful directions gaining momentum right now, and a lot of them translate really well into dining rooms specifically.

The good news is that even if you're not ready to repaint, most of these trends can be introduced through textiles, accessories, and art — which means you can stay current without committing to a full decorating project.

Current and Trending Colour Directions for Dining Rooms

  • Warm earthy tones: Terracotta, warm sand, raw clay, and rust are at the height of their popularity right now — and they photograph beautifully too.
  • Moody deep greens: From sage to forest to emerald, green continues to be the most versatile and trend-resistant colour in interiors.
  • Warm off-whites and putty tones: The move away from cool, stark whites continues — warm plaster tones and limewash finishes are leading the way.
  • Chocolate brown and caramel: Rich warm browns are having a genuine moment in interiors right now — paired with cream and brass, they feel luxurious without being cold.
  • Seasonal shifts through accessories: Keep a neutral or warm base year-round and swap out textiles, candles, and ceramics seasonally — richer tones in autumn and winter, lighter fresher ones in spring and summer.
Pro Tip: For an easy seasonal refresh, keep a box of dining room accessories in seasonal colours. A set of deep burgundy linen napkins and amber glass candle holders can completely shift a room from summer-fresh to autumn-cosy in under ten minutes. It's one of the most cost-effective decorating habits I know.

Inspiring Dining Room Colour Styles: From Japandi to Maximalist

Sometimes seeing a room rather than reading about it is what finally clicks everything into place. Below you'll find a curated selection of dining room colour looks across a range of styles and palettes — from calm and minimal to rich and layered.

More About Building a Complete Dining Room Colour Palette

A great dining room colour palette is never just about the paint — it's the full picture of colour, texture, light, and layers working together.

If you want to see how professional designers and colour experts approach this, it's worth exploring resources that go deep on the topic. For instance, The 24 Best Dining Room Colors, According to Designers offers a really strong visual reference for how different colours read in real dining rooms across a range of styles — useful for pressure-testing your own ideas before you commit.

What I'd add to any expert advice is this: always start with something you already love — a piece of art, a fabric, a ceramic — and build outward from there. The palette that emerges will feel coherent precisely because it's rooted in something real and personal to you, rather than assembled from trend boards and paint charts alone.

WATCH: 10 Perfect Dining Room Paint Colors – Ideas & Inspiration

Your Dining Room, Your Colour Story

If there's one thing I hope you take away from all of this, it's that choosing a dining room colour palette doesn't have to feel like a high-stakes decision. Start small, start with what you love, and let the room evolve naturally from there.

You don't need to do everything at once. A rug and a print can transform a space. A painted sideboard can change the whole conversation. And when you're ready to paint, you'll be doing it with real confidence because the palette will already feel like yours — not something you borrowed from a paint brand's catalogue.

The most memorable dining rooms I've ever worked in weren't the ones with the biggest budgets or the most perfect colour combinations. They were the ones that felt genuinely lived-in and personal. That's always the goal.

So tell me — is there one colour you've always wanted to try in your dining room but haven't quite had the courage to go for yet? I'd love to know what's holding you back.

Knowing how to frame contemporary art is one of the most satisfying things you can do for your home — get it right and a single piece can transform an entire room. The good news is that it is absolutely something you can do yourself, even if you have never picked up a mount cutter in your life. This guide walks you through every step, from choosing the right frame style to hanging the finished piece on your wall.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in front of a beautiful piece of wall art and felt completely stumped about how to frame it without ruining what makes it so special?

Quick answer: To frame contemporary art well, choose a clean, minimal frame in a material and colour that complements rather than competes with the piece. Use a generous mount if the work is on paper, select UV-protective glazing, and match the frame's proportions to the artwork's scale. DIY framing is very achievable with the right tools and a bit of patience.

Contemporary art covers a huge range of styles — abstract paintings, bold graphic prints, photographic works, mixed-media pieces and more. What they tend to share is a visual energy that deserves a frame that works with it, not against it. Whether you are shopping for unique wall art or already have a piece on your hands, framing is the step that makes it look truly finished. The same goes for broader unique home decor — the way you present things matters just as much as the things themselves.

Choosing the Right Frame Style for Contemporary Art

The frame style you choose sends an immediate visual signal, so it is worth thinking about this before anything else. Contemporary art generally calls for either a minimalist frame that stays out of the way, or a carefully chosen traditional frame that creates a deliberate contrast.

[[IMG|choosing-frame-style-contemporary-art|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A bright, airy living room with white walls, a low-profile natural oak sideboard topped with a small ceramic vase and a trailing pothos plant, a textured linen sofa in warm oatmeal tones, and a slim natural wood floating shelf on the wall. On a round side table sit two frame samples — one sleek black aluminium frame and one ornate gilded wooden frame — laid flat for comparison. A Black British woman in her early thirties, casually dressed in a cream roll-neck jumper, sits cross-legged on the sofa examining the two frames with a thoughtful expression.]]

Minimalist vs Traditional Frames: Which Suits Contemporary Art?

  • Minimalist frames (thin profiles, clean lines, metal or plain wood) let the artwork lead — ideal for abstract work, bold colour-field pieces, and photography.
  • Floater frames give canvas work the illusion of floating in mid-air, which suits contemporary painting beautifully.
  • Traditional ornate frames can work brilliantly with contemporary art as a deliberate juxtaposition — a heavy gold frame around a raw abstract can feel very intentional and gallery-like.
  • Box frames work well for mixed-media or textured pieces that need a little depth between the art and the glazing.
  • Avoid frames with lots of decorative carving unless you specifically want the contrast effect — they can visually compete with bold contemporary work.

I once helped a client who had a stunning large-format abstract in rich terracotta and ochre tones. Her instinct was to find a frame that matched those warm colours exactly. We tried it — and honestly, it looked fussy and crowded. The moment we switched to a slim natural oak floater frame, the painting breathed. The rule I always come back to is: the frame should hold the artwork, not join it.

Pro Tip: Visit a local gallery and look at how they hang contemporary work — most use very thin, simple frames or no frames at all on canvas. That restraint is not laziness; it is a deliberate choice to keep attention on the art.
